ai-at-work.title: It’s hot IPO summer, and the MANGOS are ripe
ai-at-work.excerpt: The IPO market is back, and it’s not the same companies leading the charge. FAANG had a good run, but a new acronym is taking over: MANGOS — Meta (or Microsoft, depending on who you ask), Anthropic, N
ai-at-work.dwp_take: A bunch of hot AI and tech companies are heading to IPO at roughly the same time, replacing the old FAANG guard with a new acronym nobody asked for. For digital workplace folks, this matters because whatever these companies build or acquire will eventually show up in your tech stack, whether you want it or not. Honestly, I'm less interested in the acronym and more interested in which of these outfits will actually build something useful for offices instead of another chatbot that needs constant babysitting.

ai-at-work.title: ChatSee raises $6.5M to build ‘failure memory’ for enterprise AI agents
ai-at-work.excerpt: ChatSee.AI Inc., a company that provides a failure intelligence layer for autonomous artificial intelligence systems, today announced it raised $6.5 million in seed funding. True Ventures led the roun
ai-at-work.dwp_take: ChatSee just raised 6.5 million bucks to build systems that remember when AI agents mess up, so they don't keep making the same mistakes. This matters because every digital workplace is about to have AI running loose in their systems, and right now those AI agents are basically goldfish with send buttons. If we're going to let machines make decisions about our work, having something that actually tracks and learns from failures beats the hell out of crossing our fingers.

ai-at-work.title: SpaceX’s record IPO, Bezos’ Prometheus rising and Anthropic’s controversial call for AI limits
ai-at-work.excerpt: Blastoff! Elon Musk’s SpaceX went public Thursday evening and raised a stunning $75 billion, easily an all-time record. The IPO is just the first of the triumvirate of AI leaders — yes, SpaceX owns xA
ai-at-work.dwp_take: SpaceX just pulled off a record $75 billion IPO, with a chunk of that valuation coming from its AI division xAI, while OpenAI and other AI companies are gearing up for their own public debuts. This matters to digital workplace folks because these companies are literally building the tools and infrastructure that will shape how we work, communicate, and collaborate over the next decade. Honestly, watching billionaires race to monetize AI while calling for "limits" on AI is peak 2024 energy, and we're all just trying to figure out which tools will actually stick around long enough to justify the hype.

ai-at-work.title: Elon Musk’s SpaceX raises record-breaking $75B after pricing IPO at $135 per share
ai-at-work.excerpt: Elon Musk’s Space Exploration Technologies Corp. has priced its initial public offering at $135 per share ahead of one of the most hotly anticipated market debuts in living memory. The rocket company
ai-at-work.dwp_take: SpaceX just pulled in $75 billion through its IPO at $135 per share, making it one of the biggest market debuts ever. For digital workplace folks, this matters because SpaceX's success signals investor confidence in tech-heavy companies with demanding engineering cultures, which shapes how other tech employers think about remote work, collaboration tools, and talent retention strategies. Honestly, if SpaceX can go public at that valuation while running on Slack and email like the rest of us, maybe we can finally stop pretending our workplace software choices actually move the needle.

tools-tech.title: 40% of enterprises will scrap AI agents - 3 ways to ensure yours don't fail
tools-tech.excerpt: How do you create real ROI from autonomous AI? Three digital leaders share lessons they've learned in the field.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Forty percent of enterprises are expected to abandon their AI agent projects, though some companies have figured out what actually works. This matters because most organizations are throwing budget at AI without a clear strategy, and watching competitors fail is the cheapest education available right now. Here's the thing: enterprises love shiny objects, so half of them will deploy AI agents badly, declare them broken, and move on to the next trend while the smart ones quietly build real value.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft’s Patch Tuesday updates: Keeping up with the latest fixes
tools-tech.excerpt: Long before Taco Tuesday became part of the pop-culture vernacular, Tuesdays were synonymous with security — and for anyone in the tech world, they still are. Patch Tuesday, as you most likely know, r
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft released its monthly security patches on Patch Tuesday, addressing vulnerabilities across Windows, Office, SQL Server, and other products. For digital workplace professionals, staying current with these updates is non-negotiable because one unpatched system can become the entry point that brings down your entire organization's security posture. After thirty years in this business, I can tell you that the companies getting breached aren't the ones patching on Tuesday, they're the ones who decided to patch "when we get around to it."

tools-tech.title: For June, Patch Tuesday means an IT scramble
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft this week released 206 updates affecting Windows, Office, Exchange Server, and its developer tools — including three Windows vulnerabilities already publicly disclosed. That trio includes an
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft dropped 206 patches this month, including three Windows zero-days that were already out in the wild before the fix arrived. For digital workplace teams, this is a reminder that your patching process needs to move faster than a snail on sedatives, because bad actors are actively exploiting known holes. Nothing quite like spending your June afternoon explaining to leadership why we need an emergency patching cycle instead of waiting for the next scheduled window.

tools-tech.title: French government’s secure messaging system breached
tools-tech.excerpt: An intruder has breached the French government’s encrypted messaging service, Tchap, showing once again that human error is a weak spot in any security system. Tchap was developed in France as an exam
tools-tech.dwp_take: A hacker broke into France's government-only encrypted messaging app, Tchap, which was built specifically to avoid relying on WhatsApp and prove French tech independence. This matters to digital workplace pros because it's a perfect case study in how security theater fails when you ignore the actual weakest link: the people using the system. After three decades in this space, I can tell you that building a Fort Knox messaging app is pointless if your users are still writing passwords on sticky notes and clicking phishing links.

industry-news.title: Apple’s Mac Studio Cheat Sheet: Features, Pricing, Specs, and More
industry-news.excerpt: Learn what the Mac Studio is, how much it costs, M4 Max vs. M3 Ultra differences, key specs, use cases, limitations, and buying advice. The post Apple’s Mac Studio Cheat Sheet: Features, Pricing, Spec
industry-news.dwp_take: Apple released the Mac Studio with M4 Max processors, updated specs, and new pricing tiers, positioning it as a workstation alternative for creative professionals. For digital workplace managers, this matters because hardware choices directly impact productivity, security posture, and total cost of ownership across your organization. Here's the thing though: most companies will still struggle justifying Mac Studio to their CFO, and rightfully so, unless they've got legitimate creative workflows that actually demand it.

industry-news.title: Microsoft Restricts Claude Fable 5 Access Amid AI Safety Review
industry-news.excerpt: Microsoft reportedly limited internal use of Claude Fable 5 while legal teams review Anthropic’s 30-day data-retention policy. The post Microsoft Restricts Claude Fable 5 Access Amid AI Safety Review
industry-news.dwp_take: Microsoft has hit the brakes on internal Claude Fable 5 access while its legal team reviews Anthropic's data retention practices, particularly around a 30-day policy. This matters because enterprises are already nervous about which AI tools they can safely deploy in their workplaces, and when a major tech company's own legal team pumps the brakes, it sends a real signal about data governance concerns. Honestly, it's refreshing to see someone actually ask "where does our data go?" before rolling out AI at scale, even if it does slow things down.

industry-news.title: CISA Warning: LiteLLM Flaw Could Expose Enterprise AI Gateways
industry-news.excerpt: CISA’s LiteLLM warning shows why AI gateways and agents need service account governance, scoped access, credential rotation, and audit trails. The post CISA Warning: LiteLLM Flaw Could Expose Enterpri
industry-news.dwp_take: CISA flagged a vulnerability in LiteLLM that could let attackers bypass enterprise AI gateway protections if service accounts aren't properly locked down. This matters because most organizations rushing to deploy AI are treating security like an afterthought, and a compromised gateway means someone could be asking your AI anything they want without permission. After thirty years in this space, I've watched the same pattern repeat: shiny new tech arrives, security gets bolted on later, and someone's resume gets updated.

industry-news.title: China’s EV Giants Race Tesla to Mass-Produce Humanoid Robots
industry-news.excerpt: Chinese EV makers, including BYD and XPENG, are racing Tesla to commercialize humanoid robots, betting that physical AI will become the next big market. The post China’s EV Giants Race Tesla to Mass-P
industry-news.dwp_take: Chinese EV manufacturers like BYD and XPENG are pushing hard to mass-produce humanoid robots, competing directly with Tesla's robotics ambitions as they bet on physical AI becoming a major commercial market. This matters to digital workplace folks because humanoid robots will eventually reshape how we think about automation, workspace design, and what jobs actually need humans in the office. Personally, I'd rather see them solve the basic problem of getting my company's collaboration software to work reliably before we're all sharing cubicles with robots.
